strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: evaluating instruction-following capabilities of multimodal large language models across speech, video, and text in crosslingual scenarios.
The experimental setup includes a wide spectrum of 21 open-source models, spanning text-only LLMs, SpeechLLMs, VideoLLMs, and omni/multimodal LLMs.
The evaluation setup systematically considers context length (short-form vs. long-form) and prompt robustness (fixed prompts vs. mixed paraphrased prompts).
weaknesses: Incomplete submission: The manuscript is visibly unfinished. Section 5 explicitly includes a notice stating 'WARNING! This section contains intermediate and incomplete results', and Sections 5.2 ('Effect of Modalities Integration') and 5.3 ('Breakdown on Question Answering') contain only placeholder text ('Work in progress...'). In addition, several paragraphs in Section 5.1 are left incomplete.

Very small sample size: The core benchmark is based on only 21 presentations (~2 hours of video) and 220 question-answer pairs. Given the fine-grained breakdown across 13 tasks, 4 languages, and multiple modalities, the statistical support per subset is extremely limited, making performance numbers highly susceptible to high variance and noise.

Lack of human evaluation or validation of metrics for QA and summarization: The benchmark evaluates open-ended generation (QA and summarization) solely using rescaled BERTScore against single references, which can correlate poorly with factual correctness and nuance in complex scientific contexts.

Reproducibility and transparency of data creation: The dataset annotation relies on confidential internal ASR and MT engines provided by a commercial language service agency prior to post-editing, which introduces uncontrollable artifacts and limits reproducibility.

strengths: Ambitious benchmark motivation: Bridging multilingual and multimodal instruction-following across video, audio, and text in both short and long contexts is an important and timely direction.
Extensive model suite: Evaluates a diverse collection of 21 open-weight models across text-only LLMs, SpeechLLMs, VideoLLMs, and omni/multimodal LLMs.
Involvement of human annotation: Transcripts and translations were handled by professional linguists, and QA pairs were curated by domain experts rather than relying entirely on synthetic generation.

strengths: The benchmark addresses a timely and relevant problem: evaluating large multimodal models (MLLMs) across speech, vision, and text in cross-lingual, instruction-following, and both short- and long-context settings.

The data curation process involves professional human transcription and translation, as well as carefully categorized human QA annotations with explicit labels for required modalities (audio, video, AV, unanswerable).
Extensive baseline evaluations are conducted across 21 diverse open-weight models categorized into LLMs, SpeechLLMs, VideoLLMs, and omni MLLMs.
Evaluating both fixed (`MCIF_fix`) and varied (`MCIF_mix`) prompt formulations provides useful insights into instruction robustness and sensitivity to phrasing.

The benchmark size for the core tasks is relatively small: only 21 scientific presentations (~2 hours of video) and 220 question-answer pairs are evaluated for recognition, translation, and QA, which limits statistical significance and domain diversity.

The cross-lingual evaluation is strictly unidirectional: all original presentations, speech, and video contexts are in English, with only the instructions/outputs translated into target languages (German, Italian, Chinese). It does not test comprehension of non-English spoken or visual content.

Reliance on rescaled BERTScore for open-ended question answering and summarization across diverse target languages can be brittle and sensitive to response lengths/formatting; validation via human evaluation or LLM-as-a-judge correlation is missing.

strengths: Comprehensive Multi-Modal and Cross-Lingual Setup: The benchmark uniquely bridges text, audio, and video modalities across four typologically diverse languages (English, German, Italian, Chinese) under both short- and long-context scenarios.

Careful Parallel Alignment and Design: Because input and target references are aligned across modalities and languages, MCIF allows clean diagnostic ablations isolating the exact contribution and interference of individual modalities (e.g., speech alone vs. speech+video).

High-Quality Human Curation: QA pairs are annotated with precise modality dependencies (Audio-only, Video-only, Audio-Visual, Not Answerable) by domain experts, while transcriptions and translations were verified and translated by professional linguists rather than relying entirely on synthetic generation.

Extensive Empirical Evaluation: Evaluates 23 diverse open and proprietary models across LLMs, SpeechLLMs, VideoLLMs, and omni/MLLMs, providing valuable diagnostic insights such as the struggle of current omni-models to effectively fuse visual and audio information.
weaknesses: Limited Dataset Size and Diversity: The core benchmark comprises only 21 talks (~2 hours of video) and 220 QA pairs (with an expanded set of 100 talks limited to summarization). All data comes strictly from ACL 2023 NLP presentations, limiting domain diversity and generalizability beyond academic presentations.

English-Centric Source Material: All input video and audio are exclusively sourced from English talks, with multilingualism introduced via translation of text, prompts, and outputs; this does not test non-English speech or culturally diverse visual/video inputs.

Reliance on BERTScore for Open-Ended Evaluation: Using only BERTScore for open-ended QA and summarization can fail to capture fine-grained factual correctness, penalize semantically valid paraphrases, or overlook verbosity and hallucination issues compared to hybrid metrics or LLM-as-a-judge / human evaluations.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely gap by providing a fully aligned, parallel multimodal (text, audio, video) and crosslingual benchmark for instruction following.

Rigorous manual data curation and annotation process involving professional translators and domain experts, including careful categorization of QA pairs by modality dependence (Audio-only, Video-only, Audio-Visual, Unanswerable).
Extensive experimental evaluation across 23 state-of-the-art models spanning four model paradigms (LLMs, SpeechLLMs, VideoLLMs, and MLLMs).

Insightful analysis providing concrete takeaways, notably that joint audio-video processing often degrades performance compared to single-modality inputs in current MLLMs, and that prompt variation (Fix vs. Mix) causes notable performance instability.
weaknesses: The dataset size for core fine-grained tasks is relatively small: only 21 talks (~2 hours) and 220 QA pairs, which limits statistical power and diversity of speaker domains.
Crosslinguality is strictly unidirectional from English: all source presentations are in English with prompts/outputs in DE, IT, and ZH, leaving non-English source comprehension unaddressed.

Evaluation for open-ended QA and summarization relies primarily on BERTScore, which may not adequately capture fine-grained factual correctness, entity accuracy, or hallucination in complex scientific domains compared to LLM-as-a-judge or human evaluation.

strengths: Well-motivated benchmark design: MCIF addresses critical gaps in the literature by uniting three modalities (speech, video, text), four languages, and both short- and long-context evaluation within an instruction-following setup.

High-quality, human-annotated data: The dataset relies on professional linguists and translators for transcripts and translations, and domain experts (NLP/ML researchers) for question-answering pairs, avoiding common synthetic or contaminated data pitfalls.

Fully parallel cross-modal structure: Because content is aligned across text, speech, and video, the benchmark allows clean ablation studies isolating the exact contribution and failure modes of individual modalities and multi-modal fusion.

Extensive experimental evaluation: The paper benchmarks 23 diverse models (LLMs, SpeechLLMs, VideoLLMs, MLLMs) and compares fixed vs. paraphrased prompts (MCIFfix vs. MCIFmix), revealing insightful findings regarding long-context degradation and multimodal integration bottlenecks.
weaknesses: Limited dataset scale for core tasks: The multimodal question-answering and recognition tasks are based on only 21 talks (around 2 hours of content) and 220 QA pairs. While 79 talks are added for summarization, the relatively small sample size for QA limits statistical robustness across granular sub-analyses.

Unidirectional crosslingual setting: The source content is exclusively English-language scientific presentations, with multilingual evaluation restricted to prompts and target responses (en -> de, it, zh). It does not test multi-source or non-English speech/video inputs.

Reliance on BERTScore for open-ended tasks: QA and summarization evaluation relies primarily on BERTScore. For technical scientific content, incorporating exactness/factuality metrics, LLM-as-a-judge, or targeted human correlation checks would strengthen the evaluation reliability.

Under-explored evaluation of unanswerable questions: Although the QA annotation schema explicitly includes an 'NA' (unanswerable) category to test hallucination, the paper lacks a detailed quantitative evaluation specifically assessing models' precision or calibration on unanswerable instances.
